Its Calls to Action also created a roadmap for governments, schools, and communities to continue reconciliation efforts in the future.

By fostering a national dialogue and establishing the 94 Calls to Action, this pillar creates a sustainable framework for systemic change and mutual respect between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. Ultimately, long-term healing is only possible when a society collectively acknowledges the truth of its past to prevent such tragedies from ever being repeated.

rationales.description:
The Mi’kmaw Treaties of 1778 and 1779 were important agreements between the Mi’kmaq people and the British government during the American Revolutionary War. These treaties were created to keep peace between the Mi’kmaq and the British and to make sure the Mi’kmaq would not join the American rebels in fighting against Britain.
The Treaty of 1778 was written and signed at Fort Howe, which is now part of Saint John, New Brunswick. The treaty was organized by Michael Francklin, the British Superintendent of Indian Affairs in Nova Scotia. He met with Mi’kmaq leaders from several communities, including Richibucto, Miramichi, and Chignecto. The Mi’kmaq chiefs signed the treaty on behalf of their people, while British officials signed it for the Crown.
A second treaty was signed in 1779. This agreement renewed the promises made in 1778 and included Mi’kmaq leaders from other communities in the region. Like the earlier treaty, it was arranged by British officials and signed by both Mi’kmaq representatives and British authorities.
The main purpose of these treaties was to maintain peace and friendship. The Mi’kmaq agreed not to support the American rebels, and the British promised to continue peaceful relations with the Mi’kmaq. The treaties also recognized that the Mi’kmaq could continue hunting, fishing, and using natural resources to support their way of life.
One of the most important facts about the 1778 and 1779 treaties is that the Mi’kmaq did not give up their land. Unlike many later treaties in Canada, these agreements focused on peace, cooperation, and trade rather than land surrender.
Today, the treaties remain important because they are still recognized by Canadian law. They help protect Mi’kmaw treaty rights and are an important part of the history of Atlantic Canada.

This fish can represent the resilience, strength, survival and balance that must be maintained in the wild due to its incredible journey up the rivers and down to the sea. The Mi'kmaw people held the Salmon with the utmost respect and only killed the animal when it was needed, either for food or to preserve it for the winter. This shows the importance that the Mi'kmaw people placed on living with nature, rather than in control of nature. The colors of this piece can be said to illustrate the importance of the Salmon, and nature itself, to the Mi'kmaw peoples. The strong hues of bright orange and yellow have ties to the color yellow meaning life,energy and warmth, as well as reminding people of sunshine and fire, which are both incredibly important in the daily lives of the Mi'kmaw peoples. The color blue surrounds the fish and reminds people of the rivers and seas that the fish inhabit, and the black outline helps to make the Salmon "pop" while paying homage to traditional art styles used in Indigenous art.

rationales.title: “Learning Through Language: A Mi’kmaw Children’s Book”
rationales.description:
For my Mi’kmaw independent project, I am creating a children’s book for my niece. This project is very meaningful to me because she is Indigenous, and I want her to grow up learning about her culture, language, and identity in a way that feels personal and accessible. Throughout this course, I have learned a lot about Mi’kmaw history, values, and ways of life, and I want my book to reflect that learning in a simple but respectful way. I chose words that are used in everyday life as well as words that carry deeper cultural meaning so a child can begin to understand both language and connection to Mi’kmaw identity.

Some of the most important words I included in my book are Msit No’kmaq, Kasapskuk (Wampum belt), Plamu, and Tu’wa’timk. I chose Msit No’kmaq, meaning “all my relations,” because it is a key teaching in Mi’kmaw culture. It reminds us that everything is connected, including people, animals, land, and water, and teaches respect for all living things. I also included Kasapskuk (Wampum belt) because wampum belts are important symbols of agreements, history, and storytelling, showing how knowledge and responsibilities are passed down through generations.

Another important word I chose is Plamu (Atlantic salmon). I included this because salmon has been an important food source and part of Mi’kmaw life for generations. It reflects the strong relationship between the Mi’kmaq people and the land and water. I also selected Tu’wa’timk (lacrosse), which is a traditional game still played today. It represents teamwork, community, and cultural continuity.

Overall, these words help connect language, culture, and identity. My goal is for my niece to not only learn Mi’kmaw words, but also understand the meaning and values behind them.

rationales.title: Quill Drop Earrings
rationales.description:
The porcupine is a delicate and defensive creature who walks their land. To the Mi’Kmaq people the porcupine represents strength and self protection because the porcupine is a kind, harmless animal equipped with a shield of quills for protection. Quill drop earrings aren’t just a way to show off indigenous culture, identity, and story telling but it connects the person wearing them to the ground they live on and the strength and worth they hold inside of themself. 

Traditionally Mi’Kmaq quill drop earrings were made from birch bark and porcupine quills that have been gathered after porcupine shed. They would start by cleaning the quills to remove all dirt and oils then the quills would have been boiled with roots, flowers or other types of organic dies. From there they would be flattened between finger nails or teeth, making them flexible so they could thread the end into tiny holes already made in the birch bark, fold the ends on the other side so when the bark completely dried they are secured and will not fall out. 

As traditional clothing evolved, so did the jewelry and earrings. Quill drop earrings began to involve bright colored seed beads making the earrings easier to stitch and more desirable to practice. This change of medium made the materials more excessable, the process less labor intensive, much easier and faster and more detailed and  intricate designs could be achieved with these beads. This allowed Mi’Kmaq people to express their culture and stories in a much more effective and enjoyable way but that does not mean the traditional process is still not used today.

rationales.title: The Protector(Pewitekemkewey)
rationales.description:
A dream catcher is a traditional indigenous protective talisman consisting of a handmade hoop woven with a web-like pattern and decorated with items such as feathers and beads. Good dreams pass through the center hole and slide down the feather to the sleeper. Bad dreams become tangled in the web and evaporate at sunrise. People place dream catchers in their houses, cars, hallways, or above their beds to filter out bad dreams and protect those sleeping. Dream catchers are also displayed to express indigenous heritage and to show that the Mi’kmaw were the first humans on the land.
The dream catcher, also called “pewitekemkewey,” originated with the Ojibwe. It holds deep modern and cultural significance to the Mi’kmaq today. Dream catchers represent healing, cultural reclamation, community resilience, and the lasting presence of indigenous people's ancestral territory in Mi’kma’ki.  According to traditional Ojibwe teachings, the universe is watched over by Asibikaashi, the Spider Woman. She was the fierce protector and custodian of all the people, especially the infants and the small children.When the Ojibwe nation spread across North America, women found it difficult to care for their children alone. To ensure their children’s protection, mothers and grandmothers began weaving magical webs using willow hoops and sinew to catch harm and negative dreams.materials needed to make the dream catcher are a circular hoop,a circular hoop (like a metal ring or embroidery hoop), leather or suede cord, string, craft glue, feathers, and beads.

rationales.title: A Sweat lodge ceremony
rationales.description: This Diorma shows the space within a  Sweat lodge where a traditional Indigenous Sweat Lodge ceremony would be performed. these ceremonies were performed all over the North America's by many of the indigenous populations, similar traditions can even be traced and practiced back in ancient northern south America and central America by the Olmec, Aztec, and early Mexican natives. for North American aboriginal peoples the ceremony was used to cleanse and heal the bodies of those that were afflicted with disease, the ceremony would be done in a large dome or oblong shaped tent-house made form natural wooden or bone supports draped with cloths and animal skins, the ceremony was always led by a recognized and wise elder who must know the traditions, songs , and steps taken exactly in order to properly perform the ceremony. The traditions entails one or people entering the sweat lodge where a fire pit and many stones of varying sizes would be placed, the people would sit in the lodge where they begin praying or singing, decoctions and water would be placed on the heated stones to create medicinal fumes and help to make the participants sweat more, after some time the people  will exit and begin performing more tradition rituals outside the lodge involving nother fire pit and exchanging seven stones between the lodge and outside. the indigenous people believed that the act of sweating allowed the body to cleanse itself of toxins and impurities as well as drive away ill thought and misfortune, this ceremony is  a very important part of Canadian indigenous tradition and is one of the ways that indigenous people of today can connect with old or lost culture.

rationales.title: Medicine Wheel
rationales.description: The medicine wheel is a visual represntation of the indigenous traditions, celebrations and their overall identity. It demonstrates who they are and what they have accomplished despite the challenges they have faced over many years. It is used to show materials they used to survive during both the extremely cold seasons, or the extremely hot seasons. It shows their way of life, where they lived, what they ate, how they got their food, just how they survived in general. The medicine wheel is a sacred symbol used by generations of the Idigenous people. It represents health, interconnectedness of life and the nature of existence. East (Yellow), is about spring, new beginnings, the rising sun, and childhood. South (Red) is about summer, youth, passion, and growth.West (Black) is about fall/autumn, adulthood, introspection, and the setting sun. North (White) is about winter, elders, wisdom, and the resting of the mind and body. The wheel teaches that having harmony and happiness needs balancing four essential parts of everyone. Mental, growth and clarity. Physical, body health and connection to Mother Earth. Spiritual faith, values, and connection to the Creator. Emotional feelings and the ability to process and express them. The medicine wheel also refers to ancient physical stone structures. Hundreds of these stone structures are located across North America, some being up to a thousands years old. The structures are central rock cairns, concentric rings, and radiating spokes that often align with the cardinal directions or astronomical events. To the Indigenous people, the wheel represents a map of the universe. It shows that everything operates in cycles (the seasons, human aging, the moon) and that no single part can work without the others.

rationales.title: A Tribute to the Stolen

The central figure of a woman stands as a testament to resilience, draped in cultural regalia that include symbols and designs passed through generations. These patterns are a language of identity, lineage, and survival, combating the systemic violence. By integrating mixed media elements, this piece of art achieves a tactile depth, bridging the gap between historical trauma and modern-day justice. The use of traditional symbols on the character’s clothing anchors the piece in their cultural history, honoring the vital concepts of Indigenous sovereignty and the sacredness of life. The lady in the artwork bears red clothing, in many Indigenous cultures, it is believed that red is the only color spirits can see. The incorporation of red lets the artwork symbolically calls back the spirits of missing and murdered women, allowing them a way to find their way home and connect with their mortal form. The background involving a mixture of colors portray the confusion that these individuals ponder, "Why was I targeted?" as the homicide rate for Indigenous women and girls is over 6 times higher than for their non-Indigenous counterparts. This piece demands that the viewer not just observe, but fuse their mindset to a victimized presence marked by absence, turning a national tragedy into something that could be a call for healing and accountability for all women.

rationales.title: The portrayal of Indigenous people in the media
rationales.description:
The portrayal of Indigenous people in the media has changed over time, but many challenges still remain. historically, Indigenous peoples were often represented through stereotypes that misrepresented their cultures, traditions, and ways of life. movies, television shows, newspapers, and advertisements frequently depicted Indigenous people as either aggressive warriors, helpless victims, or mysterious figures connected only to the past. These portrayals ignored the diversity and complexity of Indigenous communities and contributed to misunderstandings among the public.
One major issue with media representation is the lack of Indigenous voices in the creation of content. for many years, stories about Indigenous peoples were told by non-Indigenous writers, producers, and journalists. As a result, Indigenous perspectives were often excluded or distorted. This led to inaccurate depictions that reinforced harmful stereotypes and prejudice. Such representations can influence public opinion and affect how Indigenous people are treated in society. 
In recent years, there has been growing awareness of the importance of authentic representation. More Indigenous filmmakers, actors, writers, and journalists are sharing their own stories and perspectives. This has helped create more accurate and respectful portrayals of Indigenous peoples in the media. Modern films, television series, and documentaries increasingly highlight Indigenous cultures, achievements, and contemporary issues, allowing audiences to gain a deeper understanding of Indigenous communities.
Despite this progress, stereotypes and underrepresentation still exist. News coverage often focuses on negative topics such as poverty, crime, or conflict, while positive stories and achievements may receive less attention. This can reinforce harmful misconceptions and fail to reflect the full reality of Indigenous lives.

rationales.description: Building a wigwam and making a landscape around it represents many things I learned in Mi'kmaw 11. It shows how important the land is to the Mi'kmaq people and how there culture is connected to nature. The wigwam was built using materials from outside such as trees,birch bark, moss and sand. This taught me that the Mi'kmaq respected the land and only used what they needed. They cared for nature and made sure resources would be available for future generations. The landscape around the wigwam represents the traditional land of the Mi'kmaq. In this course I learned that the land provided food, medicine, transportation, and a place for families and communities to live. Rivers, forests, and animals were all important parts of daily life. This project also shows the importance of family and community. Building a wigwam was something people often did together. Everyone shared knowledge and helped each other. This taught me about the values of teamwork, respect, and responsibility in Mi'kmaw culture. Another thing I learned in this course is that the Mi'kmaq people have shown great strength and resilience. Even though colonization brought many challenges, Mi'kmaw traditions and knowledge have continued to survive. Today many people are working to keep these traditions going. Making a wigwam and landscape helped me understand the history, culture, and connection to the land that are important to the Mi'kmaq people. It represents the lessons I learned about respect, community, and the importance of preserving Mi'kmaw traditions for future generations.
